findings.title: Age sd experimental exceeds stated range
findings.description: The bound is STATED by the paper, not assumed by me: the enrolment sentence restricts the sample to patients 'in their 20s', which is the interval [20, 29]. For n = 28 confined to that interval the largest attainable sample SD is 4.58; the reported 5.84 is 127% of that ceiling. The paper additionally leans on a narrow age range as a design strength, criticising prior work for 'wide range of patient's age', so the narrow-age claim is load-bearing in the authors' own argument rather than incidental. Note this row does not feed the primary chi-squared test, so it does not alter the headline p-value; it is a Table 1 data-integrity problem.

findings.title: Age sd minimum span bracket
findings.description: This is a bracketing run, not a check of a paper-stated value, hence indeterminate: it quantifies how far the data would have to depart from the stated criterion. A span of 12 years (20-32) still fails; 13 years (20-33) is the first that admits SD = 6.33, and even there the SD sits at 95.6% of the theoretical maximum, which is only attainable if patients are stacked almost entirely at the two extremes of the range. A realistic unimodal age distribution would need a wider span still. Either way the sample cannot be described as 'in their 20s'.

findings.title: Chi squared expected counts below five
findings.description: Analysis-design mismatch (rulebook rule 5). Both infection cells have an expected count of 2.5, well below the conventional minimum of 5 for an uncorrected Pearson chi-squared, so the chosen test is not valid for this table; Fisher's exact test is the appropriate choice and returns p = 1.00 rather than 0.639. The paper reports no assumption check and does not mention Fisher's exact. This does NOT change the conclusion's direction: both tests are non-significant, so the substantive claim survives, but the reported p-value overstates the precision of the comparison.

findings.title: Grim age correctly refused (Table 1, Age row (both arms))
findings.description: Recorded deliberately as a documented refusal rather than omitted. Age in years is a continuous ratio measure and the paper nowhere states that ages were recorded as whole years, so GRIM is not applicable and the tool correctly declines. I did NOT re-run it with data_type='integer' to force a verdict: had ages been whole numbers, 23.9 x 28 = 669.2 and 24.3 x 28 = 680.4 would both be non-integral and would fail GRIM, but that conclusion rests entirely on an assumption the paper never makes, and asserting it would be a false accusation. The age anomaly is established instead by the SD-range check, which rests only on the paper's own stated inclusion criterion.

computed.error: GRIM does not apply to data_type='continuous'; it assumes integer observations on a bounded scale.

consequence.explanation: No claim is affected; this records why a granularity check on age was not pursued.

findings.title: Power analysis not reproducible
findings.description: Recorded as a refusal with its reason, not as a pass. Two observations that do not require any computation. First, the paper writes 'a test power β= 0.20': beta is the Type II error rate, so the power is 1 - beta = 0.80, and calling beta the power is a terminology error. Second, and more substantively, the stated design was sized to detect a difference between a 5% and a 35% infection rate, i.e. 30 percentage points. The observed contrast was 3 of 28 versus 2 of 28. A trial powered only for a 30-point difference cannot support a claim that no difference exists.
findings.location: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'Therefore, this study was undertaken'

anchors.quote: Twenty eight patients were enrolled in each group. The samples were selected at a significance level of α= 0.05 and a test power β= 0.20. A smaller infection rate was set to 5%, and the difference in the estimated infection rate was set to 30%, based on previous report that the incidence of postoperative wound infection using prophylactic antibiotics, ranges from 5.6% to 33.4%.

findings.title: Negative conclusion without interval
findings.description: This is the paper's headline claim and it is an absence-of-evidence inference: a non-significant p from a 5-event trial is treated as evidence that postoperative antibiotics are unnecessary. The largest effect still compatible with these data cannot be bounded from anything the paper prints, because no interval is reported. The recalculation incidentally recovered a Fisher odds ratio of 1.56, i.e. the point estimate actually favours the arm that received postoperative antibiotics, but with 5 events in total the interval around it would be very wide. Severity is asserted, not computed: nothing here is arithmetically impossible, and the concern is inferential.

findings.title: Unblinded subjective outcome assessment (Patients and Methods, paragraphs 1-2)
findings.description: Design context bearing on how much weight the 3-versus-2 event counts can carry. The trial was explicitly unblinded (no placebo), all operations were performed by one surgeon, and two of the four CDC criteria the authors adopted are subjective, one of them being diagnosis by the surgeon. Allocation itself was by Excel-generated codes, which is a reasonable randomisation method, so the concern is assessment rather than allocation. Severity is indeterminate because this is a qualitative judgement about bias risk, not a numeric anomaly, and it is asserted rather than computed.

findings.title: No attrition or flow reporting (Patients and Methods, paragraph 1; Results throughout)
findings.description: Reporting gap recorded under rulebook rule 7. All 56 enrolled patients appear in the analysis with no exclusions, withdrawals or losses to follow-up mentioned, and there is no CONSORT flow diagram or trial registration number. Complete retention is not implausible over a 2-week postoperative window in a surgical cohort, so this is noted as a transparency gap rather than treated as a signal in itself. Note the group sizes 28/28/56 are not suspiciously round in the 50/100 sense, so no round-N concern arises.
